newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-Hard man Prebble may hold key in NZ poll.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Hard man Prebble may hold key in NZ poll.

text.p: The bovver boy of New Zealand politics, Richard Prebble, believes his free-market Act New Zealand Party will be pivotal in the October 12 election.

Prebble, one of the most colourful characters on the political scene, began his career on the left of the spectrum in the Labour Party but now leads the "New Right" Act party which advocates reducing the state's role to the bare essentials.

"The objective that I am seeking is to have a big enough vote so New Zealand does not have a risky left-wing coalition," Prebble told Reuters. "This election is going to turn around on how well Act does."
The ruling conservative National Party appears able to muster 40 percent support at most and desperately needs allies to bring it near or over a majority.
Prebble believes Act, possibly in conjunction with the morals-based Christian Coalition, can deliver that.
Latest polls give Act between four and six percent, near the five percent threshold needed to win any seats on a proportional basis. The Christians are also close to five percent.
However, Prebble said Act's own polling puts it around eight percent. Because most Act supporters come from two-worker families, phone pollsters underrepresent their support, he said.

As insurance, Prebble is contesting the Wellington Central electorate where polls show he has a realistic chance in a close three-horse race. If he wins, Act will be certain of gaining seats even if it fails to clear the five percent hurdle.
"The most important issue in any election is the economic direction of the country. Act is a very strong supporter of the view that we would stay on our steady economic course," he said.
"An economic U-turn would be a disaster."

While Act may not, in coalition with National, get through any of its radical proposals for a voucher-based education system, privatisation of health and so on, it will act as a brake on government spending, Prebble said.
Act would, for example, would support the government's move to directly fund schools rather than via a ministry.
"Equal opportunity" remains his guiding philosophy but experience as a minister in David Lange's government of the 1980s led to a road-to-Damascus type conversion on achieving it.

"The experience of being in charge of 20 percent of the total investment in New Zealand when I was running the State-Owned Enterprises brought it home to me that the government is hopeless at running businesses -- much worse than most critics on the Right actually say," Prebble said.

Former Finance Minister Sir Roger Douglas was architect of the Lange government's free market reforms and Prebble the driver. Sometimes riding roughshod over virulent opposition, he pushed through privatisation and other controversial reforms.
The party was rent over economic direction with Lange first sacking Prebble in 1988 over privatisation before ditching Douglas and then resigning himself.

Prebble joined Act, founded by Douglas, in 1994 and his superior political skills were recognised when he took over as leader earlier this year. He modified Act's plan to abolish income tax in favour of a 19.5 percent flax tax as he pitched its appeal to "middle New Zealand".
Portrayed by cartoonists and satirists as a pit-bull terrier and profiled in a magazine as "the mad dog of politics", Prebble said his reputation is built on tough decision-making.

"I'm prepared to take tough decisions but I don't think I am a hard man. If somebody gives me a whack I am quite capable of responding. But I would plead that I am a counterpuncher, not a hit-man," he said.
He also rejects critic's claims that Act is the mouthpiece of big business, which is reported to have heavily funded Act.
In less than three years it has gained 14,000 members, making it the second largest party, and donations average less than $100 each, Prebble said.

"It's not the North Shore millionaire party but in fact is supported by very hard-working Kiwis. I make no apologies for being pro-business. The private sector which creates the wealth." -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
